Triaged Swap Reality Check — Parity & Rollout Demo

Redwood AE + SE walked Solstice Financial through a practical parity mapping and rollout strategy to migrate three vendor endpoints to the Redwood API. The discussion covered output equivalence checks, latency SLOs, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, VPC/KMS requirements, and a proposed benchmark plan. Agreement to run a 48hr traffic replay and provide SOC2/security artifacts; next steps include a pilot quote and scheduling a bench-run with real traffic.
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Solstice CTO), Tom Brenner (Eng Mgr), Priya Singh (Infra Lead), Elliot Park (ML Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial): Walkthrough of parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Discussed cost/latency, KV cache behavior, canary routing, and compliance artifacts. Agreed on replay benchmark and sending security docs.

Transcript:
00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining — um so we're gonna run through a practical parity and rollout plan, feel free to interrupt, especially questions on infra.
00:14 Anika: yeah thanks Maya, we wanna make sure we don't regress on hallucinations or latency. we're running OpenAI for prod chat and Together for some fine-tuned stuff.
00:26 Diego: got it, and quick intro from my side — Diego, SE, i'll cover the console, runtime differences, and the benchmark plan.
00:40 Tom: quick note, timeline wise we're aiming for a pilot in Q4, need to prove cost parity or better.
00:52 Maya: perfect, that's realistic. so first, parity mapping — we usually map model families and tokenization differences, and then run output-equivalence tests not exact match but semantic parity.
01:12 Elliot: when you say semantic parity, can you walk through an example? like our question answering outputs are pretty sensitive to phrasing.
01:23 Diego: sure so, we run a three-pronged check: 1) safety/guardrails, 2) content equivalence (embedding and rerank score similarity), 3) response latency and token usage. the console shows a heatmap of response divergence.
01:44 Priya: how accurate is the token accounting? Together uses their own tokenizer sometimes, are you normalizing tokens?
01:55 Diego: there can be tokenization drift; we normalize at ingest, run per-model token counts, and give you token delta reports. small mismatches are expected, we flag anything >10% delta.
02:12 Anika: okay, next - security. we need SOC2, iso, sso via SAML, and KMS for envelope keys — do you support customer-managed keys?
02:26 Maya: yes we do. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM, and even in Dedicated we can integrate your KMS. i'll attach the KMS integration notes in the follow-up.
02:38 Tom: great, what about audit logs and retention?
02:43 Diego: audit logs exist in the console, you can export them to your SIEM. retention is configurable for Dedicated/Private, hosted has a standard retention that we can extend as an add-on.
02:58 Anika: cool. on the runtime side, we care about p95 latency under 300ms for simple prompts — is that realistic on your hosted offering?
03:12 Diego: depends on model choice and sequence length. for smaller non-streaming prompts, our hosted API on the s-2 family achieves low hundreds p95. if you need strict p95 < 300ms at scale, Dedicated or pinned GPUs with our low-latency kernels is recommended.
03:31 Priya: what's the tradeoff on cost? Dedicated sounds pricier but predictable — we'll need cost modeling.
03:39 Maya: yep, Dedicated has a base reservation + utilization model; we also recommend quantized variants for cost without much perf loss. Redwood Optimize gives specific quantization and batching profiles per workload.
03:55 Elliot: about quantization — do you preserve determinism? some of our existing pipelines rely on deterministic outputs for tests.
04:05 Diego: quantization can introduce minor nondeterminism; we capture that in the parity tests. if determinism is required we recommend either keeping fp16 variants or locking down seeds and runtime configs for the rollout.
04:25 Maya: let's pivot to a concrete migration path — three steps: 1) compatibility layer: adapter to map endpoint inputs (OpenAI/Together/Anthropic) to Redwood API, 2) run traffic replay for 48 hours to compare outputs and cost, 3) staged rollout with canary and automated fallback.
04:50 Tom: for the adapter, how much change on our side? we already use OpenAI-compliant wrappers.
04:58 Diego: we have an adapter library that is drop-in for the common OpenAI endpoints. Together sometimes needs small mapping for metadata fields; Anthropic chat format mapping is also automated. the console's 'adapter checker' will surface mismatches.
05:15 Anika: can we keep both vendors during canary and route some percentage?
05:20 Maya: absolutely, smart routing lets you split traffic by percentage, latency/region, or by token cost. you can do 10% live on Redwood and keep 90% on your current provider to compare.
05:34 Elliot: on outputs — do you do reranking or embedding comparisons automatically?
05:38 Diego: yes we run embedding similarity and compare top-k responses; we present a regression score. if it exceeds thresholds we block promote.
05:52 Tom: curious about KV cache behavior — we're heavy on session state.
06:00 Diego: our KV cache is optimized for continuous batching; you'll see improved throughput. caveat: cache semantics differ slightly by model; during parity run we measure session latency and cache hit rates.
06:20 Priya: networking — if we do Private, we need VPC peering and egress controls; does your private control plane require inbound connections?
06:31 Maya: Private can be deployed into your VPC or we peer into it; depends on your compliance posture. inbound is minimal; most flows are outbound from a hardened subnet but we'll provide a network diagram.
06:45 Anika: what about PII handling? we have regulated PII and need redaction before storage.
06:53 Diego: we can do inline redaction or token-level masking. also we support no-persist configurations where no request/response is stored in the control plane.
07:10 Tom: ok good. demo time? show the console parity dashboard?
07:15 Diego: yeah i'll share screen — bear with me while i pull up the parity lab.
07:32 Diego: (screen) here is an adapter check run: you can see token deltas by model, similarity scores, and a per-prompt pass/fail. that pass/fail is configurable by your thresholds.
07:54 Anika: i like the per-prompt drift view. can we export failed prompts for review?
07:58 Diego: yep exportable as csv, and you can flag for retrain or prompt-tune.
08:10 Maya: quick interjection — historically most customers see eqiv within 80–95% after small prompt tweaks. big regressions usually come from differences in safety filters or tokenizer edge cases.
08:28 Elliot: what about cost modeling on actual traffic?
08:33 Diego: the console runs a simulated cost model using token deltas + quantized runtime profiles. we'll run that against your sample traffic during the replay.
08:44 Tom: sounds good — let's talk about the replay — what do you need from us?
08:49 Diego: primarily an anonymized traffic dump, similar to what you mentioned in the email: 1M tokens or subset representing typical prompt lengths, annotate streaming vs non-streaming endpoints, and mark any golden responses you want preserved.
09:06 Maya: we'll provide a replay template; the replay runs in our sandbox Dedicated or in Private depending on your preference. we advise using Dedicated for realistic perf numbers.
09:18 Priya: bandwidth — will the replay hit our egress caps? we have burst limits.
09:24 Diego: replay can be rate-limited to avoid bursts; we can stage at 10–20% of real-time to keep within caps.
09:33 Anika: ok, on acceptance criteria — besides p95 latency and semantic parity, we need to ensure no new privacy leaks or increased hallucination rates.
09:46 Maya: agreed, we'll include hallucination/regression metrics in the parity report, and safety test suites can be run as part of the replay.
10:00 Tom: any vendor lock-in risk if we adopt Redwood-specific features like KV cache?
10:07 Diego: you can opt into Redwood runtime features, but adapter patterns keep your abstractions portable. KV cache semantics are well-documented; you can keep an adapter layer to isolate usage.
10:20 Maya: moving on — pricing. i'll give a rough pilot estimate now: for a 2-week replay in Dedicated with memory-optimized instances and a small reserved capacity, estimate ballpark $X — we'll put real numbers in the quote after we know token volumes and chosen model flavors.
10:43 Anika: can you give a delta vs our current spend? we need to show finance.
10:49 Maya: we'll run a cost-parity spreadsheet: current provider invoice + your sample traffic vs Redwood's simulated cost from the console. often customers see 10–30% CPU/token savings after batching and caching.
11:05 Elliot: do you support streaming responses + function/tool calling like we use now?
11:10 Diego: yes, streaming and function calls are supported; the console test harness can replay function call patterns and measure end-to-end latencies.
11:23 Priya: observability — token-level traces and per-route SLO dashboards?
11:29 Diego: yes token-level cost, per-model latency, traces; you can hook to your tracing stack.
11:40 Tom: curious about fallback — if Dedicated runs out, do you have automated fallback to hosted?
11:46 Maya: yes that's part of smart routing, we can fallback to a compatible model family in hosted or another region; fallback rules are configurable and can be automatic with alerts.
11:59 Anika: let's discuss an edge case: our Together fine-tuned model occasionally returns structured JSON that is validated downstream. parity failures there are unacceptable.
12:12 Diego: for structured outputs we recommend schema-enforced generation + function-calling patterns. our function-calling tends to be stable; we'll run stricter tests for that sample.
12:30 Elliot: will you run a dev-to-prod smoke? small canary then traffic ramp?
12:34 Maya: yes recommended path: adapter + replay -> canary (5–10%) -> ramp -> full + rollback policy. we'll help with runbooks.
12:48 Tom: what's a typical timeline for us to get a pilot live? we want to align with Q4.
12:53 Maya: if you send the sample traffic within this week, we can start a replay within 7–10 business days, then a 48-72hr replay and a results meeting. so pilot kickoff late Sep/early Oct looks feasible.
13:07 Anika: ok, that's promising. any legal or procurement blockers we should expect?
13:13 Maya: standard enterprise terms apply; we can provide a sample MSA, and for Private deployments we have addenda for data residency. procurement sometimes requests pen-testing reports; we have those available.
13:26 Priya: SSO — we use SAML with attribute mapping for roles. how are RBAC roles mapped?
13:33 Diego: RBAC maps to SAML attributes; the console allows policy templates and custom roles.
13:43 Elliot: one last technical: do you support pinned model versions for audits?
13:48 Diego: yes model version pinning and immutable deployments are part of Dedicated/Private.
13:56 Maya: okay quick recap — agreed items: you'll share sample traffic + redaction notes; we'll share SOC2/security pack and a replay plan; we'll run a 48hr replay in Dedicated sandbox and produce parity and cost reports.
14:14 Tom: and we'll review results and decide next steps after the replay.
14:20 Anika: thanks — looks like a clear path.
14:22 Maya: great, i'll follow up with the security docs and replay template. anything else?
14:30 Elliot: maybe just to confirm, do you have a recommended default model mapping for our mix?
14:34 Diego: yes i'll include a mapping table in the replay plan (openai/gpt-x -> rdx-s1 etc), and note quantized variants.
14:46 Maya: awesome. thanks everyone, we'll send calendar invites for the bench kickoff once dates confirmed.
14:52 Anika: thanks all.
